$comment: The Arduino benchmark suite. Each entry is ONE prompt you hand ayin in an empty directory, plus
the traps that prompt sets and what a correct answer must contain.
WHY THE TRAPS ARE THE POINT. Any model can emit a blink sketch. What separates a useful Arduino
agent from a plausible one is the small set of facts that are invisible in the code and expensive
in the world: analogWrite on a pin with no hardware PWM compiles perfectly and gives you eight
colours; an LED without a series resistor works right up until it doesn't; delay() inside loop()
makes a button unresponsive in a way that reads as a hardware fault; a common-anode RGB LED needs
inverted logic. Every project below is chosen for the traps it sets, and they escalate.
`grep` entries are checked against the sketch source, `notGrep` must NOT appear. `components` are
arduino_db ids the wiring diagram is expected to match. Run with: node tool/arduino-bench.mjs

projects.title: Blink
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino project that blinks the board's built-in LED once per second.
traps: No external component at all — the wiring diagram must say so honestly rather than inventing an LED and a resistor.
LED_BUILTIN is a core macro, not a #define in the sketch, so pin resolution must leave it as-is instead of guessing a number.

projects.title: RGB cycle with a toggle button
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino project with an RGB LED that goes green → yellow → red over 10 seconds and then starts over. Pressing a button stops or starts this behaviour.
traps: Three colour channels need three PWM pins. On an Uno that is 3, 5, 6, 9, 10 or 11 — anywhere else analogWrite silently degrades to on/off.
Each channel needs its OWN series resistor. The catalog says so on the leg; a diagram without them is wrong, not terse.
Yellow is red+green mixed, not a colour the LED has. A plan that treats it as a third channel has misunderstood the part.
The button must stay responsive across a 10-second cycle, so the cycle cannot be built from delay().
A mechanical button bounces; a naive digitalRead toggles several times per press.

expect.$grepNote: the per-channel-resistor trap is checked in the DIAGRAM (three SERIES_ nodes), not the source — a resistor is a physical part and appears in no sketch.

projects.title: Pedestrian crossing
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino traffic light with red, yellow and green LEDs on its own timing, plus a pedestrian button that requests a crossing. The request must be remembered until the next safe point in the cycle, not acted on instantly.
traps: This is a state machine. Written with delay() it cannot register a button press during the phase it is sleeping through — the classic beginner failure, and it presents as 'the button doesn't work'.
'Remembered until the next safe point' means a latched flag, not a poll at the moment of transition.
Three separate LEDs, three separate resistors.

projects.title: Automatic night light
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino night light: an LDR measures how dark the room is and an LED fades up smoothly as the light drops. Print the sensor reading to the Serial Monitor so I can calibrate the threshold.
traps: An LDR is not a sensor with an output pin — it is half a voltage divider, and needs a fixed resistor to ground. Wiring it straight to an analog pin reads noise.
analogRead returns 0–1023, analogWrite takes 0–255. Feeding one to the other directly is a four-times-too-bright bug that compiles.
The LED must be on a PWM pin to fade at all.
Serial.begin's baud has to match whatever the README tells the user to open the monitor at.

projects.title: Reaction timer
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino reaction timer. After a random delay the LED lights up; the player presses the button as fast as they can and the reaction time in milliseconds is printed to the Serial Monitor. Detect and call out a press that happened before the light.
traps: 'Detect a press before the light' is the whole exercise — it needs the button watched DURING the random wait, not only after it.
randomSeed from an unconnected analog pin, or every run has the identical 'random' sequence.
Timing must come from millis()/micros() deltas, not from counting loop iterations.
Debounce, or one press reports two reaction times.

projects.title: Potentiometer-controlled servo
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino project where turning a potentiometer moves a micro servo to the matching angle, and the current angle is shown on the Serial Monitor.
traps: Servo.h owns its pin — it never calls pinMode or digitalWrite, so a pin-usage extractor that only looks for those finds nothing. `.attach()` is the signal.
map(0..1023, 0..180) — the pot's range and the servo's are unrelated numbers.
A servo under load browns out a USB-powered Uno; the README should say to power it separately and share ground.
Servo.h uses Timer1, which disables PWM on pins 9 and 10 — so those are the wrong pins for anything else here.

projects.title: Parking sensor
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino parking sensor: an ultrasonic sensor measures distance and a buzzer beeps faster the closer an object gets, going solid under 10 cm. An LED mirrors the same warning.
traps: HC-SR04 needs a 10 µs trigger pulse and pulseIn on echo — a plain digitalRead returns nothing useful.
duration × 0.034 / 2 — forgetting the /2 reports double the distance, and it looks plausible.
'Beeps faster' with delay() blocks the measurement it depends on; the beep interval and the measurement both need millis().
A passive buzzer needs tone(); digitalWrite gives a faint click. The two types look identical.
pulseIn blocks for up to a second with nothing in front of the sensor unless a timeout is passed.

projects.title: Room climate display
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino project that reads temperature and humidity from a DHT sensor and shows them on a 16x2 I2C LCD, updating a couple of times a second at most. Show a clear message on the LCD while the first reading is still pending.
traps: TWO third-party libraries that must actually be installed — the plan has to name `arduino-cli lib install` for both, and the README has to as well, or the project does not build on anyone else's machine.
A DHT11 cannot be polled faster than about once per second; reading it in a tight loop returns NaN.
The LCD's I2C address is 0x27 or 0x3F depending on the manufacturer. Hardcoding one without saying so is a blank screen with no error.
I2C is A4/A5 on an Uno — fixed pins, not a choice.
A failed read returns NaN, which prints as 'nan' on the LCD rather than failing loudly.

expect.compilesNote: needs `arduino-cli lib install "DHT sensor library" "LiquidCrystal I2C"` first — this project tests whether ayin TELLS you that

projects.title: Eight-LED bar from three pins
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino project that drives eight LEDs as a level meter from a potentiometer, using a 74HC595 shift register so it only costs three Arduino pins. The bar should fill from the bottom as the pot turns up.
projects.$componentsNote: standard-led is deliberately NOT expected in the diagram. The eight LEDs hang off the shift register's Q0-Q7 outputs, not off Arduino pins, and the diagram shows what the CODE drives — the register's own catalog note carries 'Q0-Q7 → LEDs, each through its own resistor'. Attempt 1 grounded the register and the pot correctly and was marked down for this; the expectation was wrong, not the diagram. Following the chain downstream of an IC is a real open question, recorded in RESULTS.md rather than papered over.
traps: Eight LEDs, eight resistors — one per output, not one shared on the common line, or brightness changes with how many are lit.
shiftOut with latch held LOW then pulsed HIGH; latching per bit makes the bar flicker visibly.
MSBFIRST vs LSBFIRST decides which end of the bar fills — a 50/50 guess that looks like a wiring mistake.
OE must be tied LOW and MR tied HIGH or nothing lights, and neither is visible in the sketch.
A bar graph is a bitmask built from the level, not eight separate digitalWrites.

projects.title: Addressable strip with modes
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino project driving a WS2812B strip of 30 LEDs with three modes cycled by a button: a slow colour wash, a chase, and solid warm white. The button must respond immediately in every mode.
traps: WS2812B at full white draws about 60 mA per LED — 1.8 A for 30. USB cannot supply that; the README must say external 5 V with a shared ground, or the board browns out and resets.
The strip wants a ~330 Ω resistor on the data line and a big capacitor across its supply — neither appears anywhere in the code.
'Responds immediately in every mode' rules out delay() entirely; every animation must be a millis()-driven state machine.
FastLED/Adafruit_NeoPixel is a third-party library that has to be installed.
Data goes into DIN at one end of the strip — a reversed strip is silent, not an error.

expect.compilesNote: needs a NeoPixel/FastLED library installed — the point is whether ayin says so before you find out

$rationale: Ladder 1 covered digital I/O, PWM, analog-in, non-blocking timing, ultrasonic and I2C. Repeating
that with different components would measure sampling noise, not skill. Ladder 2 goes at what
ladder 1 never touched, and every project is chosen for a trap that has NO analogue in ladder 1:
interrupts and volatile        · a counter incremented in an ISR and read in loop()
the Steinhart-Hart equation    · float maths on a chip with no FPU, from a resistance reading
a transistor as a switch       · a load an Arduino pin physically cannot drive
mains-adjacent relay safety    · the one project where wrong wiring is dangerous to a person
quadrature decoding            · two pins whose ORDER carries the information
multiplexed display refresh    · persistence of vision, where delay() is visible as flicker
UART on a second serial port   · SoftwareSerial, and TX/RX crossing over
projects.title: Motion alarm with a latching siren
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino motion alarm: a PIR sensor triggers a buzzer siren that keeps sounding for 30 seconds after the last movement, and an LED shows armed/triggered state. Use an interrupt for the PIR so motion is never missed while the siren is running.
traps: An interrupt handler must be attachInterrupt on pin 2 or 3 on an Uno — no other pin can do it, and the code compiles happily on the wrong one.
A variable shared between an ISR and loop() must be `volatile`, or the compiler caches it in a register and loop() never sees the change. This is the classic silent interrupt bug.
An ISR must not call delay(), Serial.print() or tone() — it must set a flag and return.
The HC-SR501 has its own onboard retrigger jumper and a 3-300s delay pot; the README has to say the software timer is in addition to that hardware behaviour, or the timings will not match.
'Keeps sounding for 30 seconds after the LAST movement' is a resettable timer, not a fixed 30s pulse.

projects.title: Thermistor thermostat with hysteresis
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino thermostat: read the temperature from a thermistor, print it in Celsius to the Serial Monitor, and switch a relay on below 20 C and off above 22 C. The two thresholds are deliberate — the relay must not chatter around a single setpoint.
traps: A thermistor gives a RESISTANCE, not a temperature. Converting needs the divider maths and then Steinhart-Hart (or a beta-value approximation) — a linear map() is simply wrong and looks plausible.
The AVR has no floating-point unit; log() and float maths work but cost time and flash. Using double changes nothing on this chip and wastes space.
20 C on / 22 C off IS hysteresis — implementing a single 21 C setpoint makes the relay chatter, which is the failure the two numbers exist to prevent.
A relay module is active-LOW on most boards: digitalWrite(pin, LOW) energises it. Getting this backwards means the heater runs whenever the code thinks it is off.
The relay coil needs more current than a pin can source — the module has a transistor and flyback diode on board, and the README should say why you must not wire a bare relay to a pin.

projects.title: PWM fan driven through a transistor
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino project that drives a small DC motor as a fan at four speeds cycled by a button, using an NPN transistor as the switch because the motor draws more current than a pin can supply. Show the current speed on the Serial Monitor.
traps: An Arduino pin sources 20 mA; a small DC motor wants hundreds. Wiring the motor to a pin is the failure this project exists to prevent, and it does not announce itself — the pin just dies.
The transistor needs a base resistor (~1k) or the pin sees a near short.
A motor is an inductive load and needs a flyback diode across it, or the back-EMF spike kills the transistor. Nothing in the code hints at this.
The motor's supply must be external with a SHARED GROUND — a floating ground means nothing works and nothing errors.
Four speeds means analogWrite values, so the transistor's base must be on a PWM pin.

projects.title: Rotary encoder menu on an OLED
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino project where a rotary encoder scrolls a three-item menu on an SSD1306 OLED and pressing the encoder selects an item. Turning it must feel smooth with no skipped or doubled steps.
traps: A rotary encoder is QUADRATURE: the information is in the ORDER of the two edges, not in either pin alone. Polling one pin with digitalRead gives direction that is wrong half the time.
'No skipped steps' means CLK belongs on an interrupt pin (2 or 3 on an Uno), not in a polled loop that is also driving a display.
The encoder's own switch needs INPUT_PULLUP and debouncing, like any button.
The SSD1306 is I2C on the same fixed A4/A5 as any other I2C device, and its address is 0x3C or 0x3D — NOT the 0x27 an I2C LCD uses. Confusing the two gives a blank screen with no error.
Redrawing the whole OLED every loop iteration is slow enough to make the encoder feel laggy — the display should only be redrawn when the selection actually changes.

expect.compilesNote: needs Adafruit_SSD1306 + Adafruit_GFX installed — the point is whether ayin names them before you find out

projects.title: Multiplexed two-digit counter
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino project that counts 00-99 on two 7-segment displays, incrementing once per second, with a button that resets it to zero. Both digits must appear lit at the same time without visible flicker.
traps: Two digits on shared segment pins means MULTIPLEXING — light one digit, switch, light the other, fast enough that persistence of vision fuses them. There is no way to light both simultaneously.
The multiplex refresh must be faster than about 100 Hz per digit or the flicker is visible. Any delay() in the loop shows up as flicker, which is the trap.
A common-cathode display lights a segment with HIGH; common-anode needs LOW. The catalog says which this part is; guessing gives an inverted display.
Every segment needs its own current-limiting resistor — one resistor on the common pin makes brightness change with how many segments are lit.
The one-second count and the millisecond multiplex are two independent timers; neither can be a delay().

projects.title: IR remote controlled lamp
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino project where a TV remote controls a lamp through a relay: one button toggles it, and two others step the brightness of a separate LED up and down. Print each decoded remote code to the Serial Monitor so unknown buttons can be learned.
traps: IR codes are specific to the remote in the user's hand — the sketch CANNOT hardcode codes it has never seen. The 'print each code so unknown buttons can be learned' clause is the whole design: it must ship a learning path, not invented constants.

The IRremote library's API changed substantially between v2 and v3+ (IrReceiver.decode() vs irrecv.decode(&results)). Writing v2 code against an installed v3 fails to compile in a way that reads like a broken install.
The receiver's pinout is NOT standardised across manufacturers — the catalog says to check the silkscreen, and reversing VCC/GND destroys it.
IRremote uses a hardware timer that conflicts with analogWrite on some pins (notably 3 and 11 on an Uno) — the dimmed LED must avoid whichever timer the library claims.
A relay module is active-LOW on most boards; a toggle written the obvious way runs the lamp inverted.

expect.compilesNote: needs IRremote installed; also tests whether ayin says WHICH major version its code targets

projects.title: Bluetooth soil-moisture logger
projects.prompt: Create an Arduino project that reads a soil moisture sensor every five seconds and sends a reading over an HC-05 Bluetooth module to a phone, accepting a single-character command back to change the interval. Keep the USB Serial Monitor working at the same time for debugging.
traps: 'Keep USB Serial working at the same time' forces SoftwareSerial on two other pins — the Uno has ONE hardware UART and it is the USB port. Using Serial for both is the mistake the requirement is built to catch.
TX and RX must CROSS: the module's TX goes to the Arduino's RX. Wiring straight-through is silent, and it is the single most common HC-05 failure.
The HC-05's logic is 3.3V on RX; feeding it 5V from an Uno needs a divider or level shifter. The catalog says so; the code cannot.
SoftwareSerial cannot reliably do 115200 on a 16 MHz AVR — 9600 is the safe default, and the HC-05's factory default is 9600 for data but 38400 in AT mode.
A resistive soil sensor corrodes if left continuously powered; the README should mention powering it from a pin only while reading.
Reading every five seconds while staying responsive to an incoming command means neither may block.
